decisions.reason: Leaf-cutting ant foraging on Eucalyptus grandis is compared across fungal inoculation methods and untreated plant controls. Preserve treatment context when assessing individual observation eligibility.

Atta sexdens colonies receive different plant diets; plant-specific acceptance during acclimation and subsequent substrate acceptance are reported. Body spot-check identifies heat sterilization and mixed diets that require observation-level review.
Wheat zinc biofortification study; Atta Habib is a wheat genotype, with no leaf-cutting ant behavior.
Fungal species descriptions and collection substrates. Mention of fungus isolated from leaves inside an Atta nest does not describe plant-substrate choice or rejection.
Ant embryogenesis and segmentation study, without plant-substrate behavior.
Van Atta antenna-array engineering study; Atta is unrelated to the ant genus in this context.

Reports leaf-cutting ant attack on named host and non-host plant species. Retain for extraction of explicit observed plant use and any contextual behavioral reports; host terminology alone does not establish rejection.
Review of ant combat, recruitment, and battle tactics; the behavioral endpoint is inter-ant competition rather than plant-substrate choice.
Atta texana temperature sensing and thermal preferences for fungus growth, without plant-substrate choice.
Insecticide detoxification in Megachilidae bees; wrong focal taxon and no leaf-cutting ant plant-substrate behavior.

Review of fungal pathogen application for pest-ant control, with mortality and colony inactivation endpoints. Its abstract and spot-checked behavioral discussion concern pathogen defenses and bait application rather than plant-substrate choice.

Acromyrmex experiment measures bait acceptance and subsequent fresh Acalypha leaf cutting, including control colonies. Retain for natural leaf observations while preserving fungal exposure and manufactured-bait context.
Rose leaf selection by solitary leafcutter bees for nest construction; wrong focal taxon for the Atta/Acromyrmex pilot.
Atta sexdens hygiene responses to fungal exposure, including fungus grooming and weeding; no plant-substrate choice endpoint is described.

Samples plant fragments actively foraged by free-ranging Atta colombica and studies provisioning choices. Field acceptance observations are relevant regardless of the nutrient-toxin hypothesis outcome.
Atta sexdens cutting preference is compared between endophyte-colonized and control Eucalyptus urophylla plants. Preserve inoculation status when assessing natural-substrate evidence.
Acromyrmex nest architecture, ventilation, and carbon dioxide concentrations; plant material is discussed as nest covering, without fungal-food substrate choice.
Acromyrmex chooses artificial sticks by thickness during turret construction; physical building-material selection is outside fungal-food plant-substrate behavior.

Compares grass- and dicot-cutting Atta fungus gardens in relation to harvested substrate. Retained as a borderline source for explicit plant-use or secondary behavioral observations, although the abstract mainly describes microbiomes.
Ant karyotype and cytogenetic survey; no plant-substrate behavior.
Human meditation and creative cognition study; ATTA denotes a creativity test, not the ant genus.
Computational and behavioral study of ant traffic priority rules; the endpoint is trail organization rather than plant selection or rejection.
Ethnobiological study of human consumption and collection of edible insects, including Atta; does not study leaf-cutting ants choosing plants.
Flower preferences and pollen transport by cavity-nesting solitary bees; wrong focal taxon for the Atta/Acromyrmex pilot.
Atta sexdens vibrational orientation and multimodal communication. Substrate here means the physical medium transmitting vibration, not plant food choice.

Examines carrying and handling of orange pellets under cycloheximide treatment and subsequent untreated feeding. Retained as a borderline substrate-behavior source; manufactured baits and treatment effects require observation-level exclusion or separate labeling.

Compares vegetation carried into Atta sexdens nests with vegetation removed and discusses recognition during substrate quality control. Also includes inoculated rice, which requires distinct treatment context.
Acromyrmex carbon dioxide preferences for fungus-garden placement and worker location; no plant-substrate choice.
Gallery construction and prey capture by Azteca and Allomerus plant-ants. Atta workers are experimental prey or intruders, not plant-substrate foragers in this study.

Atta and Acromyrmex behavioral responses to a named plant's essential oil are directly tested. Retained conservatively as a borderline behavioral source; treated surfaces and isolated components do not by themselves establish natural plant rejection.
